analysis.one_liner: Forgives up to $30,000 of federal student debt for borrowers who made five years of payments and worked ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal student loan forgiveness program. A borrower with a federal Direct Loan would get up to $30,000 of principal and interest cancelled after making 60 monthly payments and working, full-time or part-time, for 10 years after leaving school. The bill never moved past its initial referral to the Senate education committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who are already in repayment on a federal Direct Loan (including Parent PLUS and consolidation loans), have made 60 monthly payments under any repayment plan, and have worked at least 10 years since leaving school. For them, up to $30,000 of remaining principal and interest would be cancelled. Borrowers who already received equivalent forgiveness under another program (like Public Service Loan Forgiveness) for the same service would not be double-paid [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Education to cancel up to $30,000 of principal and interest due on an eligible Federal Direct Loan for any borrower who has made 60 monthly payments and been employed for 10 years after leaving school [S2][S3].
Counts full-time or part-time employment, and lets any authorized repayment plan count toward the 60 payments, so borrowers in standard or income-driven plans both qualify [S3].
Covers Stafford, Unsubsidized Stafford, PLUS, and Consolidation loans, extending the benefit beyond just undergraduate borrowers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The cancelled balances — up to $30,000 per qualifying borrower — would simply be extinguished from the federal loan portfolio, with no offsetting spending cuts or tax increases in the bill [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, through the loan program

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no funding mechanism or offset: up to $30,000 per qualifying borrower would be added to the federal deficit, and the bill sets no limit on how many borrowers could qualify [S3].
It helps only borrowers who reach both milestones: someone who has made 60 payments but not yet worked 10 years, or who left the workforce, gets nothing under this program [S3].
Broad loan forgiveness can feed expectations of future cancellation, which critics argue encourages schools to keep raising prices — a cost eventually borne by students and taxpayers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a borrower carrying $30,000 or more of federal student debt after years of payments, this would be meaningful relief worth real money. The trade-off is straightforward: the cost is added to the federal deficit with no offset, and the benefit is uneven — it rewards borrowers who stayed employed for a decade and skips those who defaulted or left work early. Whether that trade is worth it is a fair policy debate; this bill never entered that debate, because it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on May 26, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No cosponsors joined — the bill ended with zero [S4].
After the referral, no further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired in committee [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan borrowers got no relief from this bill, so the status quo held: lenders and servicers continued collecting on the full balances, and the Treasury kept receiving interest payments that forgiveness would have wiped out. Taxpayers avoided the cost.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan division ever registered on the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: Cancelling up to $30,000 per qualifying borrower would remove balances servicers collect fees on, shrinking the pool of loans in repayment. Servicers' financial interest in this bill ran against borrowers' relief, though the bill never advanced far enough to affect them.

industries.industry: Lenders and investors holding securitized student debt
industries.note: Forgiveness extinguishes principal and future interest that would otherwise flow to the loan program and its financing. A smaller loan portfolio means less revenue backed by student debt.
